public_rationale: In context, Zitron is answering the boast that agents will automate large parts of work. He says agents are not the 'totally autonomous AI that can do an entire job' they are sold as, and he cites 58% and 35% success rates himself. So 'don't work at all' is fairly read as 'do not work as dependable autonomous workers', not 'never succeed'. On that reading the evidence before the post supports him. Salesforce's own CRMArena-Pro benchmark found leading agents managed only about 58% single-turn and about 35% multi-turn success on realistic business tasks, and its authors describe a substantial gap from enterprise needs. A separate CMU-led benchmark found the best agent completed 30% of workplace tasks. METR found frontier models could finish roughly 50-minute software tasks half the time. That shows real but unreliable bounded capability, which would refute a literal zero-capability reading but not the contextual one.
limitations: The result depends on reading 'at all' as hyperbole. Read literally, the claim is false: even the speaker's cited source shows partial success.
Benchmarks may understate value in supervised, human-in-the-loop use.

statement.excerpt: Agents don’t work! They don’t work at all.
statement.document_title: How To Argue With An AI Booster

from_speaker: said in reply to 'Agents will automate large parts-'
'agent' has now become a mythical creature that means 'totally autonomous AI that can do an entire job'
cites Salesforce research: ~58% success on single-step tasks, 35% on multi-step
agents are not autonomous, they do not replace jobs
our_interpretation: Read in context, 'don't work at all' is not a claim that agents never succeed at any task. The speaker himself cites 58% and 35% success rates in the same passage. The plain reading is that AI agents do not work as boosters describe them: they cannot reliably and autonomously complete multi-step work or do an entire job.
Test: did the best available measurements before the post show agents failing to complete realistic multi-step professional tasks reliably and autonomously?
Target period: January 2025 to the post date (August 2025). This is the most recent state public evidence could report before the post.
criteria.support_condition: Independent or credible benchmark evidence from the period shows that leading agents fail a large share of realistic multi-step business or workplace tasks, well short of dependable autonomous job performance.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible evidence from the period shows that agents reliably and autonomously complete realistic multi-step professional work at high success rates, or do whole jobs.

evidence.excerpt: Experiments reveal leading LLM agents achieve only around 58% single-turn success on CRMArena-Pro, with performance dropping significantly to approximately 35% in multi-turn settings.
evidence.explanation: Leading agents failed about two-thirds of realistic multi-turn business tasks. That supports the contextual claim that agents do not work as dependable autonomous workers.

evidence.excerpt: find that the most competitive agent can complete 30% of tasks autonomously. This paints a nuanced picture on task automation with LM agents--in a setting simulating a real workplace, a good portion of simpler tasks could be solved autonomously, but more difficult long-horizon tasks are still beyond the reach of current systems.
evidence.explanation: An independent workplace benchmark found the best agent completed 30% of tasks autonomously, with long-horizon tasks out of reach. This fits the contextual reading. It is context only because this abstract version is dated after the post.

evidence.excerpt: On these tasks, current frontier AI models such as Claude 3.7 Sonnet have a 50% time horizon of around 50 minutes.
evidence.explanation: Frontier agents could complete roughly hour-long software tasks about half the time. This shows real but unreliable bounded capability. It would contradict a literal zero-capability reading, but not the contextual reading.
